finale.text: That's twelve stops and almost four hundred years of Boston saying no. A woman banished for holding meetings in her house. A mayor's permit to speak on the Common. A magazine sold for a half dollar, a novel sold for fifteen, a film the censors wouldn't touch, a play sent to Quincy and a musical ordered to get dressed. Then the city zoned what it couldn't ban, and the people it raided kept their bar open. Nearly every quote on this walk comes from a court record, a speech, the Society's own annual reports, a newspaper or a marker you just read. The censors kept good records. That's how we know.

pitch_60: On April fifth, nineteen twenty-six, the magazine editor Henry Mencken stood on the corner of Park and Tremont and sold one copy to the one man in Boston who wanted him arrested. He got his wish. That's stop two. Banned in Boston is a walk through almost four hundred years of this city saying no. A permit to talk on the Common. A burlesque house the police filmed in secret. A Pulitzer Prize play sent to Quincy. The state's highest court going to see Hair, then ordering the cast to get dressed. And a city marker that can't spell the theatre it's standing in front of. Every stop is a riddle that walks you to the next one, and every answer is something you read off a marker, a wall or a door. The censors kept very good records. That's how we know any of this. It ends at the Bay Village bar where Boston's first Pride march started. It starts at Park Street station. Bring a phone light for the small markers.

seo.landing_copy:
For about a hundred years, Boston was where books, plays and films came to be banned. The Watch and Ward Society told booksellers what not to sell, mayors revoked theatre licenses, the vice squad brought a camera to the burlesque, and the state took books to court by name. The phrase 'banned in Boston' became a selling point everywhere else.

Banned in Boston is a self-guided walk through that history and the places people went anyway. It starts on the Common, where a public speech once needed the mayor's permit, and runs past the corner where a famous editor got himself arrested on purpose, through the site of Scollay Square's most famous burlesque house, down Washington Street into what was the Combat Zone, and on to the Theater District stages that fought the censors. It ends in Bay Village.

It's twelve stops plus a bonus, about two and a half hours and three kilometers, flat and step-free on the main route. Each stop is a riddle that walks you to the next spot, and the answer is something you can only get by looking: a word on a marker, a year, a misspelling on the city's own marker. Then you get the story, with its sources.

The sources are the point. Court opinions, the Watch and Ward Society's own annual reports and pamphlets, the Landmarks Commission's survey of a Combat Zone building, a 1970 TV news film, the Harvard Crimson's 1929 interview with Groucho Marx. Where the sources disagree, we say so. Where a famous story is shaky, we tell it, then tell you what the record says.

Nothing explicit, 12 and up. In a hurry? The short cut does the Combat Zone and the theatres in about an hour.

Off the Bricks: Boston Hunts. Any two stops free. Start at Park Street.

story.card_text: In the 1890s you needed the mayor's permit to make a speech here. The city's ordinances said no person shall 'make any public address' on the public grounds 'except in accordance with a permit from the mayor.' A man named Davis spoke on the Common without one. His lawyer told the U.S. Supreme Court that preaching the gospel on the Common went back to 'time immemorial.' He was convicted. In 1895 the state's highest court upheld it in an opinion by Oliver Wendell Holmes, who wrote that a legislature forbidding speeches in a park was no more an infringement than it is 'for the owner of a private house to forbid it in his house.' In 1897 the U.S. Supreme Court agreed. So the Common was the mayor's living room. It took until 1939, in Hague v. CIO, for Justice Owen Roberts to write that streets and parks 'have immemorially been held in trust for the use of the public,' and that the Boston case didn't settle the question. The fountain is from 1868, the Common's first public art. Four figures, none with a permit.
story.headline: In the 1890s a public speech on the Common needed the mayor's permit, and Oliver Wendell Holmes said that was fine.
story.look_now: Look down the paths. In 1897, anyone giving a speech on them needed the mayor's signature first.
story.narration_script: You're at Brewer Fountain, just inside the Common. Start here, because this is where Boston drew its first line. Under the city's ordinances in the eighteen nineties, nobody could make a public address on the Common without a permit from the mayor. A man named Davis did it anyway. His lawyer argued that preaching the gospel on the Common went back to time immemorial. He was convicted. In eighteen ninety-five the state's highest court upheld it, in an opinion by Oliver Wendell Holmes. Holmes said a ban on speeches in a park was no worse than the owner of a private house banning them in his house. Two years later the United States Supreme Court agreed. The Common, in other words, was the mayor's living room. It took until nineteen thirty-nine for a Supreme Court justice to write that parks and streets are held in trust for the public. Now count the bronze figures around the fountain. Four of them. None with a permit.

story.card_text: On April 5, 1926, H.L. Mencken, editor of the American Mercury, stood here holding copies of his April issue. The offense was 'Hatrack,' a story by Herbert Asbury about a prostitute in his Missouri hometown. The Watch and Ward Society had called it obscene, and under an informal arrangement the Society told booksellers what not to sell and the police arrested anyone who sold it anyway. Mencken came to be arrested on purpose. A crowd Mencken remembered as mostly Harvard undergraduates watched the Society's secretary, J. Frank Chase, pay a silver half dollar for a copy. Mencken bit the coin, the story goes, and Chase had him arrested. The next day Judge James P. Parmenter acquitted him, and Mencken printed the judge's opinion himself. Now the name. Brimstone Corner sounds like hellfire sermons, and that's the story most people tell. The church says otherwise: during the War of 1812 its crypt stored brimstone, a gunpowder ingredient. story.card_text: On December 3, 1860, the anniversary of John Brown's execution, abolitionists met in Tremont Temple to ask 'How Can Slavery Be Abolished?' A mob - Douglass called it 'a mob of gentlemen' - took the stage, and the meeting was, in his words, 'broken up and dispersed by the order of the mayor, who refused to protect it.' Six days later Douglass gave a lecture at the Music Hall that became A Plea for Freedom of Speech in Boston. Two lines from it still do the work: 'Liberty is meaningless where the right to utter one's thoughts and opinions has ceased to exist.' And a suppressed speech 'violates the rights of the hearer as well as those of the speaker.' The building you're looking at isn't the one he stood in. The marker says the Temple burned three times and this one went up in 1896. It kept the job, though. On May 2, 1915, the NAACP met here against The Birth of a Nation, then rallied on the Common. More on that at stop six.

story.card_text: Boston's censoring didn't start with the Watch and Ward. It started on this lot. Anne Hutchinson lived here, and she held meetings at her house to talk over the week's sermons. In November 1637 the colony's court banished her 'as being a woman not fit for our society.' She asked why. Governor Winthrop answered, 'The court knows wherefore and is satisfied.' Her house burned in the fire of 1711, and the brick building you're looking at went up after it. From 1845 to 1865 it was home to Ticknor and Fields, who published Hawthorne, Longfellow, Stowe, Emerson and Thoreau. Then Boston's prosecutors found Walt Whitman. In 1882 James R. Osgood and Co. was publishing Leaves of Grass when the District Attorney, prodded by the state Attorney General, said two poems had to go or there would be an indictment. Osgood would keep the book only without them. It ended with Osgood handing Whitman the plates, about two hundred twenty-five copies and a hundred dollars. And in 1903, Boston Magazine reports, a clerk at the Old Corner Bookstore sold Rabelais to a Watch and Ward agent and got arrested for it.

story.card_text: Look for Hollis Street and you won't find it. In 1929 it ran west off Washington Street about here, and the Hollis Street Theatre stood on it, on the lot where the Hollis Street Church had been - the third time on this walk a church and a stage have traded places. That year the Theatre Guild had Eugene O'Neill's Strange Interlude, a Pulitzer Prize winner, booked in. Mayor Malcolm Nichols decided it was unfit for Boston, and the run was canceled. Nobody argued. Under a 1904 city law, the mayor could revoke a theatre's license, and a theatre owner who wanted to stay open didn't fight him. The Guild took the show to the Quincy Theatre, just past the city's reach, and by one account thousands went. The theatre is long gone. story.card_text: The Wilbur opened in 1914 and has been through two famous fights with the censor. In 1940 Tennessee Williams's Battle of Angels tried out here. A New York company that staged the uncensored text in 2021 says the City Council demanded an investigation, Police Commissioner Joseph F. Timilty called it 'Lascivious and immoral,' and the run was cut short. Thirty years later came Hair. Faced with prosecution by Suffolk District Attorney Garrett H. Byrne, the producers went to the Supreme Judicial Court, and each justice on the case went to see the show. On April 9, 1970, the court called it, in some degree, 'an obscure form of protest protected under the First Amendment,' and said that apart from certain scenes it was 'not lewd and lascivious.' Then it ordered 'each member of the cast be clothed to a reasonable extent.' The cast played it uncut that night anyway. The producers suspended the show rather than make the cuts, and on April 10 a WHDH-TV crew filmed the cast singing outside on this sidewalk. A federal court then barred the DA from closing it, and the U.S. Supreme Court split four to four.

story.card_text: In 1971 Boston's first Pride march started at this door, and its first list of demands was read right here - to the bar itself: women-only seating upstairs, a woman bartender, cleaner bathrooms. Then the march went on to Police Headquarters, the State House and St. Paul's Cathedral. Most of this walk is Boston saying no. This stop is the people who went anyway. Henry Vara opened a bar here in 1938 as the Colonial Tavern, says the Boston Preservation Alliance; the Leventhal Map Center says 1939. By the mid-1940s it was, at night, one of the most popular gay bars in the city. In the 1950s, Bay Village and Park Square were the center of queer Boston, and the bars along the Park Square stretch were raided by the vice squad again and again. 'It was always touch and go about the cops coming in and raiding the place,' one patron of those bars remembered; staff flashed the lights as a warning. In the 1960s City Councilor Frederick Langone said the city would be 'better off without these incubators of homosexuality and indecency.' The bar was renovated and renamed Jacques in 1964. The Alliance calls it Boston's oldest surviving LGBT establishment. The Watch and Ward folded in the late 1960s. Jacques is still pouring.

story.card_text: From 1933, the Watch and Ward kept its headquarters here. Its annual reports read like inventories. In 1906 one store raid turned up '98 pamphlets, 140 pictures, 198 glass negatives.' The 1909 report counted 4,183 pictures 'seized and destroyed by court' and blamed a dance craze: 'The advent of Salome has been the debauching agent.' In October 1929 one of its investigators paid fifteen dollars for a copy of Lady Chatterley's Lover at a Cambridge bookshop, and the Society's 1930 pamphlet on the case bragged that it had won 'not less than ninety-eight percent' of its cases in ten years. By the 1960s the state did the job itself: Massachusetts law let the Attorney General sue a book. In 1966 the state's highest court heard Attorney General v. A Book Named 'Naked Lunch,' called the book 'grossly offensive,' and cleared it anyway. By the historian Neil Miller's account, the Society lasted from 1878 into the late 1960s. The building went up in 1917 for the Christian Endeavor society. In the late 1990s the Unitarian Universalist Association bought it, and in 2010 its publisher, Beacon Press, published Miller's history of the Watch and Ward. He called it Banned in Boston.

story.narration_script: You're on Mount Vernon Street, outside number forty-one. From nineteen thirty-three, this is where the Watch and Ward Society kept its headquarters. Its own annual reports read like inventories. In nineteen oh-six, one store raid turned up ninety-eight pamphlets, a hundred forty pictures and a hundred ninety-eight glass negatives. In nineteen oh-nine, it counted four thousand one hundred eighty-three pictures seized and destroyed, and blamed a dance craze called Salome. In nineteen twenty-nine, one of its investigators paid fifteen dollars for Lady Chatterley's Lover at a bookshop in Cambridge. By the nineteen sixties the state did the job itself. Massachusetts law let the Attorney General sue a book, and in nineteen sixty-six the state lost to a book named Naked Lunch. The historian Neil Miller traces the Society from eighteen seventy-eight into the late nineteen sixties. Later the Unitarians bought this building, and their publisher, Beacon Press, put out Miller's history of the Watch and Ward. He called it Banned in Boston.

web.teaser: The Watch and Ward Society spent decades telling Boston what not to read. In 1933 it moved its headquarters to Beacon Hill. Decades later the same building belonged to the people whose press published the Society's history, under the title Banned in Boston. It's a private building on Mount Vernon Street; look from the sidewalk.

subtitle: The censors, the court cases, and the places people went anyway
summary: For about a century Boston had a name as the country's censor, and 'banned in Boston' sold books everywhere else. This walk runs from the Common, where a speech needed the mayor's permit, past the corner where Mencken sold one magazine to get arrested, through Scollay Square and the Combat Zone, to the theatres that fought City Hall and the Bay Village bar where Boston's first Pride march started. The censors kept good records. That's how we know.
